options.text: Outer-shell electrons free to move throughout the metal structure
options.explanation: They are not bound to any single atom.

options.text: Electrons locked into covalent bonds between atoms
options.explanation: Metallic bonding has no localised shared pairs.

options.text: Inner-shell electrons orbiting tightly
options.explanation: Delocalisation involves the outer shell only.

options.text: Free neutrons drifting between atoms
options.explanation: Neutrons stay in the nucleus.

questions.stem: What charge do the metal centres carry after their electrons delocalise?

options.text: Alternating positive and negative
options.explanation: Every metal centre is positive.

options.text: Positive - the atoms become positive ions
options.explanation: Losing electron grip leaves a net positive core.

options.text: Negative - they gain the shared electrons
options.explanation: The electrons are shared by all; each centre is positive.

options.text: Neutral - nothing changes for the atoms
options.explanation: Delocalisation is precisely the change.

questions.stem: Why does the lattice hold together despite ion-ion repulsion?

options.text: Repulsion vanishes inside metals
options.explanation: The repulsion exists but is overruled.

options.text: Neutrons cushion the ions apart
options.explanation: Neutrons are inside nuclei and play no binding role.

options.text: Attraction between each positive ion and the surrounding electron sea outweighs the repulsion
options.explanation: The sea pulls on every ion from all directions.

options.text: The ions actually attract each other directly
options.explanation: Like charges repel; the sea mediates the cohesion.

questions.stem: Which statement about delocalised electrons is correct?

options.text: They orbit fixed parent atoms
options.explanation: Delocalised means released from parentage.

options.text: They carry no charge
options.explanation: Their charge is exactly what mediates metallic bonding.

options.text: They only exist at the metal's surface
options.explanation: They roam the whole structure.

options.text: They are not bound to any particular atom
options.explanation: Belonging to the whole lattice is their defining trait.

questions.stem: A textbook diagram shows metal cations suspended in a shared electron pool. The bond holding each cation in place is

options.text: the electrostatic attraction between the cation and the delocalised electrons
options.explanation: That ion-to-sea pull is the metallic bond.

options.text: a covalent bond to its nearest neighbour
options.explanation: No fixed pairs exist in a metal.

options.text: an ionic bond to a nearby anion
options.explanation: No anions are present in a pure metal.

options.text: gravity between the heavy cores
options.explanation: Gravity is negligible at this scale.

questions.modelAnswer: Delocalised electrons are outer-shell electrons free to move throughout the metal structure, not bound to their original atom.

questions.stem: State what holds the metallic lattice together.
questions.modelAnswer: What holds the lattice together is the strong electrostatic pull between positive metal ions and the surrounding delocalised-electron sea.

questions.stem: Explain why metal atoms become positive ions when their electrons delocalise.
questions.modelAnswer: The atoms' outer-shell electrons leave to roam the whole lattice, so each atomic centre is left with more protons than locally bound electrons - a net positive charge - even though the crystal overall stays neutral.

questions.stem: Describe, in drawing terms, a correct exam sketch of metallic bonding in copper.
questions.modelAnswer: Draw rows of labelled Cu+ ions in tight layers surrounded by a labelled sea of delocalised electrons filling the gaps - and note that the electron labels are what many sketches forget.

questions.stem: Why do metals have high melting and boiling points?

options.text: Ions cannot vibrate at high temperature
options.explanation: Ion vibration is exactly what melting entails.

options.text: Strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons needs large energy to overcome
options.explanation: The ion-to-sea bonding runs through the whole giant lattice.

options.text: Covalent bonds between atoms must break
options.explanation: No directional covalent bonds exist in a metal lattice.

options.text: The electron sea insulates the ions from heat
options.explanation: Conduction, not insulation, is the electron behaviour.

options.text: Heat vibrations carry the current
options.explanation: Vibrations transfer heat, not charge.

options.text: Protons flow along the wires
options.explanation: Protons stay bound in nuclei.

options.text: Delocalised electrons move through the structure carrying charge
options.explanation: Electrons entering one end displace others from the far end, so current flows.

options.text: Ions migrate between electrodes
options.explanation: The ions are fixed in the lattice; only electrons move.

options.text: Covalent bonds stretch and reform
options.explanation: No directional bonds exist to stretch.

options.text: Ions swap places with electrons
options.explanation: Ions keep their sites; layers glide instead.

options.text: The lattice shatters and reseals
options.explanation: Shattering is brittleness - the opposite property.

options.text: Ion layers slide over one another while the electron sea maintains the attraction
options.explanation: The bonding survives the shift because the sea belongs to no particular atom.

questions.stem: Why is an alloy stronger than its pure parent metal?

options.text: Added atoms of different size disrupt the layers and block easy sliding
options.explanation: Irregular layers jam the glide that makes pure metals soft.

options.text: Alloying removes delocalised electrons entirely
options.explanation: The sea remains; it is the layer structure that is disrupted.

options.text: Alloying introduces ionic bonds
options.explanation: The bonding stays metallic.

options.text: Alloying melts and refreezes the metal stronger
options.explanation: No refreezing mechanism is involved.

questions.stem: Which change strengthens the metallic bonding in a metal?

options.text: Widening the gaps between ions
options.explanation: Distance weakens electrostatic attraction.

options.text: Increasing the number of delocalised electrons per atom
options.explanation: More sea electrons deepen the ion-to-sea attraction.

options.text: Increasing the size of the metal ions
options.explanation: Larger ions weaken the per-contact pull.

options.text: Decreasing the positive charge on the centres
options.explanation: Lower charge weakens attraction.

questions.stem: State the two packing arrangements metal ions commonly adopt in lattices.
questions.modelAnswer: Metal ions commonly adopt hexagonal layer packing or a cubic packing plan.

questions.stem: State the three changes that increase the strength of metallic attraction.
questions.modelAnswer: More delocalised electrons per atom, higher positive charges on the metal centres, and smaller metal ions.

questions.stem: Explain why metals conduct heat as well as electricity.
questions.modelAnswer: The same mobile delocalised electrons that carry charge also transport kinetic energy: speeding electrons collide with metal atoms and ions, passing thermal energy along, alongside the increased vibration of the particles themselves.

questions.stem: A jeweller wants a strong, shapeable gold ring. Explain why pure gold is chosen over a heavily alloyed wire for malleability, using the layer-sliding model.
questions.modelAnswer: Pure gold's uniform layers glide under the hammer while the electron sea re-binds each shifted layer, so the metal shapes without cracking; heavy alloying would jam those glide planes, strengthening the piece but costing workability.
